An Appetites for Risk model
(missy) An uncertain nuclear effects model
By Madeline Berzak
Blast and thermal data from
Glasstone & Dolan, 1977

P(missy) is an uncertain nuclear weapons effects model that accounts for a range of uncertainties in simulating target lethality and weapons effects that significantly affect results, and thus, analysis. These uncertainties are most often flattened into vast simplifications, only reflecting a small scene of the complex reality.

P(missy) models four common parameters within a Monte Carlo simulation method: lethal radius, p(kill) or probability of kill, p(miss) or probability of miss, and SSPK, or single shot probability of kill. These parameters are used for force posture analysis, research on weapons effects, and in understanding operational planning. In their own ways, each of the above variables are represented in formulas by a single data point, when in reality, this single data point is a range. Give p(missy) a whirl!

Checking the math against published figures

Every time this page loads it runs the calculation against figures that are already in print, carried past the digit a briefing rounds them to, and every block below names the entry under Sources it is read off so that any row here can be checked against the page it came from. Each figure is carried in whatever unit its source printed it in, which is why metres, nautical miles and feet all turn up in the same table, and it is the reason the model converts on the page rather than inside the arithmetic. If one of these rows says fail, something is wrong and nothing else on this page should be trusted.

01 · What is p(missy)?

Every input to a targeting calculation is a range, not a number.

P(missy) is an uncertain nuclear weapons effects model. Rather than solving the standard targeting math once with every input fixed at a single value, it runs that same math several thousand times over while drawing each input from the range it actually occupies, so that what comes back is a spread of answers rather than one.

The parameters it models are the familiar ones, lethal radius, SSPK, p(miss) and p(kill), and they are the numbers behind force posture analysis, research on weapons effects, and much of what is understood about operational planning. They are what an analyst reaches for in asking whether a counterforce strike could work, how much of an arsenal would survive one, and what an exchange of that kind would cost in lives. P(missy) does not alter any of those formulas; what it shows is how much of the resulting answer was decided by assumptions rather than by physics, which is something a single number can never disclose.

Those inputs are also far less settled than they appear. A hardened silo sits somewhere between 1,500 and 5,000 psi depending on which silo and whose estimate you take, wartime reliability is somewhere above 0.8 and nobody who says so can tell you where above, and accuracy is a design specification rather than a measurement of anything that has ever been done in anger. The convention is to take a value from the middle of each of those ranges and carry it forward as though it had been settled all along.

Sampling the ranges instead moves the answer, and it moves in one direction only, because the chance of a miss is raised to the number of warheads assigned to each target, which means that averaging across a range will always leave more silos standing than running the middle of that range does. The gap widens as the ranges widen, and it falls on precisely the question counterforce analysis exists to answer, which is whether the other side would have anything left to retaliate with.

A second argument runs underneath all of this. The fight over counterforce and countervalue targeting is conducted almost entirely on the fallout ledger, counting who dies downwind of a silo field, while fire is the mechanism that actually puts soot in the stratosphere, and nobody adds the two ledgers on the same page. I think the risk of a nuclear winter belongs inside targeting calculations. It isn't in them yet.

02 · What is Monte Carlo simulation?

Monte Carlo simulation was invented for this exact problem.

Monte Carlo simulation is a method for answering a question when you cannot pin down the numbers going into it. Rather than solving the problem once with a single value for each input, you solve it over and over, drawing each input at random from the range it could plausibly occupy. In other words, what happens to the answer if the accuracy is a little worse, the silo a little harder, the weather a little foggier? Run it a few thousand times and what comes back is not an answer but a distribution of answers, and the shape of that distribution is exactly what a single calculation cannot tell you.

The method and the subject grew up together. Stanislaw Ulam arrived at the modern version of it at Los Alamos in 1946, while recovering from an illness and playing solitaire. He wanted to know the odds that a hand of Canfield would come out, found the combinatorics tedious, and realized he could lay out a hundred hands and count the wins instead. The problem he actually needed it for was neutron diffusion in a weapon core, which had plenty of data and no way to be solved on paper. John von Neumann carried the idea to the ENIAC, Nicholas Metropolis supplied the name, and the first fully automated Monte Carlo calculation, in the spring of 1948, was of a fission core.

Castle Bravo is what it looks like when a range gets collapsed into a single number. Detonated at Bikini Atoll on 1 March 1954, it was predicted at 6 megatons and delivered 15. The predicted range was really 4 to 8 megatons, and some of the designers had cautioned that the yield could reach 15, but 6 was the figure that traveled. The error underneath it was one assumption: the lithium-7 in the fuel, about 60% of the lithium content, was treated as inert, and it was not. It produced tritium instead, and that tritium fused. The largest weapon the United States has ever detonated came in at two and a half times its design yield, eight years after Monte Carlo was invented in the same laboratory, because one number in the calculation was carried forward as though it were settled.

So the case for sampling rather than assuming is neither new nor abstract. What is strange is that the targeting math downstream of the weapon never took the method up. Force posture analysis is still done overwhelmingly at the middle of every range and reported as a single figure, even though the tool for doing otherwise was built in the same place, for the same reason, and is now cheap enough to run in a browser tab.

Why it suits this problem

  1. The math is cheap. One pass through lethal radius, SSPK, reliability and p(miss) takes a fraction of a millisecond, so eight thousand passes take less than a second. There was never a computational reason to avoid doing this, only a question of patience.
  2. Averaging the inputs is not the same as averaging the answers. p(miss) raised to the number of warheads is a convex function, which means the answer taken from the middle of every range sits systematically below the average of the answers across those ranges. Sampling is the only way to see that gap, and no amount of care with a single calculation will reveal it.
  3. What is worth reporting is a distribution. Anyone who needs to know the risk that twenty silos survive rather than one is asking about the tail of a curve, and a point estimate does not have a tail.
What it does not doMonte Carlo does not invent information. If the ranges going in are wrong, the distribution coming out is wrong with more decimal places attached. The method carries uncertainty through a calculation; it does not reduce it. Every range in the panel is a judgment, taken from the open literature where the literature has one, and marked in gold where it does not.

Where to read more

The first three are short, free, and written for a general reader rather than a statistician. The last is where the Castle Bravo figures come from.

  1. Eckhardt, Roger. “Stan Ulam, John von Neumann, and the Monte Carlo Method.” Los Alamos Science 15, Special Issue (1987): 131–41. mcnp.lanl.gov.

    • The origin story, the solitaire hand, and von Neumann's letter proposing the ENIAC calculation. Also the clearest short explanation of what a random number generator has to do, and why that is harder than it sounds.

  2. Metropolis, Nicholas. “The Beginning of the Monte Carlo Method.” Los Alamos Science 15, Special Issue (1987): 125–30.

    • The companion piece, by the man who named the method, on how it was actually run on the machines of the late 1940s.

  3. Metropolis, Nicholas, and S. Ulam. “The Monte Carlo Method.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 44, no. 247 (1949): 335–41. doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1949.10483310.

    • The first unclassified paper on the method and the first to carry the name. Six pages, and readable.

  4. National Security Archive. “Castle BRAVO at 70: The Worst Nuclear Test in U.S. History.” Briefing Book, February 29, 2024. nsarchive.gwu.edu.

    • The declassified record behind the yield figures above, including the General Advisory Committee minutes giving the predicted yield as four to eight megatons, and Carson Mark's explanation that lithium-7 had been assumed to be a much less good fuel than lithium-6.
03 · How to use the model

P(missy)'s presets reproduce a worked example, and then you widen it.

The model is preset to a case taken straight out of a targeting briefing: a single Minuteman III warhead at 335 kilotons and 120 metre accuracy, aimed at a silo hardened to 3,000 psi, with four warheads assigned to each silo and two hundred silos in the set. Run it as it stands and the calculation returns the same figures the briefing does, and the self-test at the foot of the model page checks every one of them against results that are already in print every time the page loads, saying so plainly if any of them drift.

Where to start

  1. Run it once exactly as it loads and read the five rows of the calculation from the top down, since that is the whole of the standard method, and the last row is the answer a briefing would report, which at these settings is about one silo of two hundred left standing.
  2. Then look at the three figures beneath it, which answer that same question three different ways: with the numbers as they are set, allowing for luck alone, and allowing for the ranges as well. The distance between the first and the third is what the model exists to show.
  3. Now widen the four pairs of boxes under Ranges, not values, taking hardness across the full 1,500 to 5,000 psi a silo can occupy, and run it again. Nothing about the physics has changed; only the honesty about the inputs has.
  4. Then go further down to Equations, not one equation, which does the same thing to the formula itself rather than to what is fed into it. Untick two of the three lethal radius formulas so that only one is in play, run it, and put them all back, because the gap between those two runs is the part of the answer that comes from nothing but a choice of published equation.

What each input means

Yield
The energy released, in kilotons. Hiroshima was about 15, and the W78 carried on a Minuteman III is 335.
CEP
Circular error probable, meaning the radius the warhead lands inside half the time, so a lower number is a more accurate missile.
Reliability
The share of missiles that launch, fly and detonate as intended. Cold War testing points to something above 0.8 for advanced arsenals, which is a floor rather than a number.
Target hardness
The blast overpressure a target absorbs before it stops working, in pounds per square inch. A silo is 1,500 to 5,000, while a road-mobile launcher is 2 to 5, and so is an ordinary house.
Warheads per target
How many warheads are assigned to each aimpoint. Assign more than one and the target survives only if every one of them misses.
Targets in set
How many aimpoints are being attacked, where two hundred is roughly the size of a silo field.
Ranges, not values
The four pairs of boxes that turn each of those numbers into a span. Everything above them is a single value, whereas these are what the model actually draws from, and widening them is the whole exercise.
Formula for the single answer
Which of the published lethal radius formulas the five rows of the calculation use. It is set to the General Electric calculator, which is the one the standard exchange arithmetic inherited, so that the single answer stays comparable to what a briefing reports.
Formulas the runs draw from
Which formulas the sampled runs are allowed to pick from, one drawn at random each time. Davis and Schilling print four different expressions for lethal radius, all of them fitted to the same test data, and at five megatons against a 300 psi target they return anything from 3,762 to 4,095 feet. That disagreement is an uncertainty like any other, and there is no reason it should be the one input a model treats as settled.
Yield exponent
How lethal radius scales with yield. Every formula here uses the cube root, 0.3333, which follows from peak overpressure alone. A silo is damaged by how long the pressure lasts as well as how high it climbs, and a bigger weapon holds it longer, so cube-root scaling understates what a megaton-class warhead does. Working back from Wohlstetter's own figures gives 0.3690 instead, anchored at 50 kt, which is the top of this range.
Seed
Any word or number. The same seed redraws the same run exactly, so a result can be quoted and checked by someone else, and it travels in the exported CSV.
Runs
How many times to run the calculation. Eight thousand is ample, and the shape of the answer stops changing well before that.

What comes back

One answer, numbers as set
A single pass with every input fixed where its slider sits, which is the number a briefing reports.
Allowing for luck only
The spread you get from chance alone, supposing the odds themselves were known exactly. This is the error bar usually quoted alongside a result, and it is the smaller of the two.
Allowing for the ranges too
The average across every run once the inputs are drawn from their ranges, with a 95% band around it. This is nearly always the largest of the three, for the reason set out under 02.
Plate 01
Twelve whole attacks on the same silo field, all drawn from the same settings, where every tick is one silo and the circled ones survived. The count at the right of each row is that attack's answer, and the disagreement between the rows is the point.
Worth holding on toOne target here means one aimpoint rather than one warhead, and a surviving silo may hold a MIRVed missile carrying several of them, so the number of surviving targets is a floor on surviving warheads rather than a count of them. That error runs in the same direction as the sampling gap does, which is toward understating what the other side would have left to retaliate with.
04 · What current models miss

What the tools in use actually account for.

This is not a complaint that models are simplified, since every model is, and simplifying is most of what makes one usable. The claim is narrower than that. The three tools the field relies on take almost entirely disjoint sets of inputs, and not one of them carries uncertainty from one stage through to the next. Most of the terms in the lower block of the table appear in none of them at all, and two of those rows are empty for p(missy) as well, along with a third for height of burst, which has no closed form available to borrow. Every cell here can be checked against the tools themselves, which is why this is a table rather than an argument.

FactorStandard exchange mathNUKEMAP Nuclear winter modelsP(missy)
The two ledgers, from one set of inputs

Push yield and height of burst down and fallout casualties fall dramatically, which is the standard counterforce result and the reason planners reach for small, accurate weapons rather than large ones. Those same two settings also govern the thermal pulse, and with it how much of the ground below catches fire, so one of these ledgers is counted with real care while the other is not counted at all.

05 · About The Effects of Nuclear Weapons

Our understanding is built on a book from 1977.

Samuel Glasstone and Philip Dolan compiled The Effects of Nuclear Weapons for the Departments of Defense and Energy, and the third edition from 1977 has become a foundational reference for blast physics and thermal dynamics in the nuclear field since its publication. So fundamental, in fact, that most of p(missy)'s numbers emerge from it. The field still uses many of the visual graphs in Glasstone and Dolan to determine the optimal height of burst (how high to detonate a nuclear weapon) that achieves a certain amount of overpressure to properly destroy a target.

Glasstone and Dolan's comprehensive work is inherently technical and dense, though its parameters and insights still remain central to policy, strategic, and operational considerations. Although the basic science around blast physics hasn't changed much, Glasstone and Dolan's research can't account for changes downstream that exacerbate uncertainties in the nuclear winter mechanism chain.

While the physical processes and parameters remain the same, problems in analysis occur when assumptions form and harden into doctrine: when a range is collapsed into a single standardized data point. Problems multiply when these assumptions are not questioned as the risk landscape has shifted over time. Keep reading to learn more about some of these assumptions:

Three assumptions

Each one is a range the field collapsed into a single number. Click on a panel to open an assumption.

Atmospheric transmittance is a technical way of expressing how much radiation (like sunlight) is able to pass through the layers of the atmosphere without being absorbed or scattered by these gases and aerosols. Put simply, when detonating a nuclear weapon, the maximum area the thermal pulse can reach outwards is limited by whether the conditions outside are sunny and clear, overcast, humid, hazy, foggy, or rainy. Think of the ignition area like a circle: the estimated area taken in conjunction with the amount of combustible material in it contributes to our estimates of how much burns and whether a firestorm is able to form.

While Glasstone and Dolan acknowledge that atmospheric transmittance varies greatly, for the purposes of their calculations they assume it is equal to 1.0: a very sunny, perfectly clear day. Their own figures put transmittance at about 0.9 on a clear day, 0.6 on a hazy one with moderate visibility, and 0.3 in fog or rain. Go from the clear day to the fog and the ignition area falls by ~67%. This difference is not insignificant, and can affect our understanding at later stages of the nuclear winter mechanism chain. Water vapor, carbon dioxide, and other atmospheric aerosols can create selective absorption bands, meaning that atmospheric transmittance is not a single number; rather it is a spectrum-dependent function.

Glasstone and Dolan brush past this assumption completely, and as a result, the field also brushes past this today.

The ignition threshold is the amount of heat a material has to absorb before it catches fire, measured as thermal fluence in calories per square centimeter. In other words, how much energy has to land on a surface before that surface starts burning? Glasstone and Dolan put the working figure at about 10 cal/cm², and that single number is what sets the ignition radius. For a 15 kiloton airburst like Hiroshima, 10 cal/cm² is reached about 2.03 kilometers out, which gives an ignition area of roughly 13 km². Every estimate built on the Hiroshima proxy starts from that circle. But the book's own tables run from 4 cal/cm² for shredded newspaper up to 50 for new bond typing paper, so the number carried forward is one value taken out of a range spanning more than a factor of ten.

There is a second problem, which is that the threshold is not a property of the material alone. It also depends on how fast the heat arrives. A fixed threshold assumes the energy is delivered instantaneously, and it is not: the thermal pulse of a 1 kiloton airburst lasts about 0.4 seconds, while a 10 megaton explosion takes more than 20 seconds to deliver its energy. Slower delivery gives heat time to conduct away before the surface reaches ignition temperature, so thick wood, wet materials and dense plastics all need more energy from a big weapon than they would from a small one. Glasstone and Dolan say as much themselves. The threshold rises with yield, and the models built on their work still use one number for every weapon.

Bigger weapons also shade themselves. In a 20 second pulse, the fires that start in the first five seconds put up smoke that shields the edge of the target area for the remaining fifteen, and surface bursts loft enough debris to cut the fluence arriving further out by 20 to 40% compared to a cleaner airburst. A static circle is being used to describe something that unfolds over time, and as usual, the reality is far more complex.

Fuel load is a term the nuclear field uses to encompass the amount of combustible material within a given target area. In other words, what could and will burn, and at what rate? Think about how cities are constructed today, versus how they were constructed in the mid-twentieth century. Hiroshima, at the time of the atomic bombing in 1945, was constructed almost entirely of wood with no more than two floors in a building. It was also confined to a clearer geographic area, unlike the vast urban sprawl of modern cities, where skyscrapers gradually melt into crowded suburbs, parks and industrial corridors. Modern cities like New York, Chicago, and Los Angeles tower with skyscrapers and dense city-centers constructed predominantly with reinforced concrete, structural steel and plate glass. We also need to think about the presence of plastics, as well as the interior contents of buildings that will also be subject to ignition.

A target list and relative nuclear winter risk constructed upon 1940s urban morphology is making an implicit bet about the atmosphere, and that bet belongs inside the targeting calculation rather than downstream of it. Which way the bet runs is not settled either. Concrete and steel are harder to set alight than the wood of 1945, while the plastics inside them give off two to three times more soot per unit mass than wood does, and those two facts pull in opposite directions.

Ignition radius at three transmittances · 15 kt airburst
Excellent visibility, clear day τ ≈ 0.9 r = √( fYτ / 4πQ ) r = √( 0.35 × 15 × 1012 × 0.9 / 4π × 10 ) r ≈ 1.94 km area = π(1.94)² ≈ 11.8 km²
Moderate visibility, hazy τ ≈ 0.6 r = √( fYτ / 4πQ ) r = √( 0.35 × 15 × 1012 × 0.6 / 4π × 10 ) r ≈ 1.58 km area = π(1.58)² ≈ 7.8 km²
Poor visibility, fog or rain τ ≈ 0.3 r = √( fYτ / 4πQ ) r = √( 0.35 × 15 × 1012 × 0.3 / 4π × 10 ) r ≈ 1.12 km area = π(1.12)² ≈ 3.9 km²

f is the thermal fraction of yield, Y the yield in calories, Q the ignition threshold in cal/cm². Between clear air and fog the ignited area falls by 67%, which is where that figure comes from.

The model at the bottom of this page runs the ignition calculation two ways. The first is the textbook version: one threshold, clear air, no spread. The second samples the ranges Glasstone and Dolan actually published, so what comes back is a spread of radii rather than a single number. To use it, set the burst mode and the thermal fraction (how much of the weapon's energy leaves as heat rather than blast), then the atmosphere, since the visibility on the day is not something anyone can know in advance, and finally the tinder mix, which decides what is out there to catch. Press run. The dashed line on the histogram is the single-number answer, and the distance between it and everything else is the point.

Figure 2.118, the fireball sequence opening 05, is from the same book, toned to the page's brown and cream. The photograph opening 01 is the Baker shot at Bikini Atoll on 25 July 1946 seen from the air, with a negative number pencilled across the print, by way of AtomicArchive; the photograph on this page shows sailors watching the same shot from a deck; the photograph opening 02 is Starfish Prime, the high-altitude shot of Operation Fishbowl on 9 July 1962, left in the colour of the original film, by way of AtomicArchive, and the photograph opening 03 is the Baker shot itself, on 25 July 1946, by way of PICRYL. The photograph opening 04 is Ivy Mike at Enewetak Atoll on 1 November 1952, converted to black and white, by way of AtomicArchive; the trails across it are smoke rockets, fired so that the blast wave would register on film. All are United States government works and in the public domain, though the exact captions and credits should be confirmed against the archive records.

Scaffold, not a finding. Parameters marked in gold have no measured basis. The forward-scatter buildup factor in particular is an approximation to a treatment G&D gives as curves. One target here is one aimpoint, not one warhead: a surviving silo may hold a MIRVed missile carrying several, so surviving targets is a floor on surviving warheads rather than a count of them. That error runs the same direction as the convexity does, toward understating what is left to retaliate with. So does one more, left out on purpose: every formula here is a cookie cutter, destroying everything inside the lethal radius and nothing outside it, where the damage functions the weapons laboratories actually used fall off gradually. Davis and Schilling put the same shot at .987 under a cookie cutter and .961 under a Sigma-20 function, and the lower number leaves more standing.

Transmittance here is Beer–Lambert on visibility with a scatter buildup term, which stands in for G&D Fig. 7.42–7.43. Ignition thresholds are log-interpolated on yield between their three tabulated columns. Not included: secondary ignitions from blast damage, smoke self-shielding of the pulse, 3-D terrain and structure shielding, fire spread, fallout.
